newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan to host world infotech congress in 2000.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to host world infotech congress in 2000.

text.p: Taiwan said on Wednesday it had edged out Australia for the right to host a global information technology congress in 2000, a privilege the government called a testament to the island's high-technology prowess.

"Getting the world-class forum to be held in our country shows that the world's information industry has affirmed our achievement in the industry," Economics Vice-Minister Lee Shu-jeou said in a statement.

Government and industrial leaders from the world's computer hardware, software, telecommunications and information service powers would attend the 12th World Congress on Information Technology, the economics ministry said.
The congress is a key gathering to review and sometimes influence global trends in information technology.
Taiwan, which beat Australia in the final selection round, will host the meeting despite China's tightening diplomatic embargo against it.

Beijing regards Taiwan as a renegade province and strenously opposes any international role by its exiled Republic of China government, but tolerates Taiwan's intimate and prosperous economic links with the world and even with China itself.

Taiwan's computer hardware industry, the world's third-biggest, is on track to grow 28.1 percent in 1996 to US$24.174 billion from $18.871 billion in 1995, the semi-official Institute for Information Industry forecast in November.
Year-on-year growth should surge 28.4 percent to $31.04 billion in 1997, 16.4 percent to $36.14 billion in 1998 and 15.7 percent to $41.82 billion in 1999, the institute said.

Lee said Taiwan would strive to complete several projects before the congress, including fully networking the government, promoting the Internet to three million users and developing a software industry zone and key information products.
The World Information Technology and Service Alliance organises the conference every two years, selecting the host country through a competition.
Inauguration ceremonies are typically hosted by the host country's leader, creating a possible opportunity for Taiwan's diplomatically embattled government, which is recognised by only 30 countries.
